texts.label: text
texts.orig: Aim: evaluate the outcomes of conservative treatment of appendicitis in young patients. Patients and methods: this study included 92 young female patients diagnosed with acute appendicitis,  eligible  patients  will  be  recruited  from  outpatient clinic, emergency department and general surgery department of Benha  University  and  general  surgery  department  of  Benha teaching hospital. Results: With a median follow-up of nine to twelve  months,  61  (66.3%)  underwent  effective  management without  surgery  and  successfully  finished  the  original  NonOperative Treatment (NOT). In the patients who failed the NonOperative Treatment (NOT) in our trial, there were no appendiceal perforations. The findings of a recent meta-analysis, which  incorporated  several  studies  regarding  the  safety  and effectiveness  of  Non-Operative  Treatment  (NOT)  in  cases  of Uncomplicated Acute Appendicitis (UAA), are in line with this. It demonstrated that Non-Operative Treatment (NOT) for Uncomplicated Acute Appendicitis (UAA) is successful, with a success rate of 66% at the last follow-up. Conclusion: Approximately half of appendicitis patients had successful conservative  treatment.  Patients  with  lower  age  and  body  mass index  but  higher  chest  problems  and  previous  GIT  symptoms exhibited more positive response to conservative treatment.

Results: With a median follow-up of nine to twelve  months,  61  (66.3%)  underwent  effective  management without  surgery  and  successfully  finished  the  original  NonOperative Treatment (NOT). In the patients who failed the NonOperative Treatment (NOT) in our trial, there were no appendiceal perforations. The findings of a recent meta-analysis, which  incorporated  several  studies  regarding  the  safety  and effectiveness  of  Non-Operative  Treatment  (NOT)  in  cases  of Uncomplicated Acute Appendicitis (UAA), are in line with this. It demonstrated that Non-Operative Treatment (NOT) for Uncomplicated Acute Appendicitis (UAA) is successful, with a success rate of 66% at the last follow-up. Conclusion: Approximately half of appendicitis patients had successful conservative  treatment.  Patients  with  lower  age  and  body  mass index  but  higher  chest  problems  and  previous  GIT  symptoms exhibited more positive response to conservative treatment.

texts.text: Introduction

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Since  it  has  been  known  for  decades  that antibiotics may be used to treat appendicitis, considering the use of antibiotics  alone  instead  of  surgery  for simple cases of appendicitis has increased. While there is a good amount of evidence to support this treatment in adults, there is still more and more data showing how safe and successful non-operative management is  for  kids.  There  is  still  a  need  for  large research, which are now being carried out with findings anticipated in the next years. The  most  frequent  surgical  emergency  in children is acute appendicitis, which has a lifetime risk of 8.6% in males and 6.7% in females.  Although  appendicitis  can  occur in any stage of life, the largest prevalence occurs in those between the ages of 10 and 19 [1] .

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Although the precise cause of acute appendicitis is still unknown, a number of ideas link it to lymphoid hyperplasia, mucosal inflammation, or the existence of a  fecalith.  The  latter  results  in  ischemia, infarction, supportive transmural inflammation, and appendix perforation by causing  luminal  blockage,  distention,  and inflammation of the appendix wall [2] . Fever,  colicky  periumbilical  discomfort, pain  migration  to  the  right  iliac  region, anorexia, nausea, and vomiting are among the common symptoms. However, because to their unusual appearance and poor communication abilities, preschoolers may be hard to diagnose with appendicitis. Almost all  of  the  120  US  children  (mean age  3.6  years)  who  were  diagnosed  with perforated  appendicitis  at  a  younger  age than  1  year  old  had  this  condition  at  the time of diagnosis, mostly due to delays in diagnosis [3] .

texts.orig: An  84%  success  rate  in  treating adult patients with uncomplicated acute appendicitis  with  antibiotics  during  their first  hospitalization  was  found  in  a  metaanalysis  of  randomized  controlled  trials that included 5 studies and 1430 individuals. Another 21 per cent of patients were  readmitted for treatmentrelated  recurrent  appendicitis  during  the follow-up year. Comparing patients receiving antibiotic therapy to those having  an  appendectomy,  there  was  an overall 39% decrease in the risk of complications [4] .

texts.orig: Sixty-one (66.3%) of them had management  without  surgery, and they successfully finished the first NonOperative Treatment (NOT), with a median  follow-up  of  nineteen  to  twentyfour months. In the patients who failed the Non-Operative  Treatment  (NOT)  in  our trial, there were no appendiceal perforations.  This  is  in  line  with  a  recent meta-analysis's findings, which incorporated  several  studies  regarding  the safety and effectiveness of Non-Operative Treatment (NOT) in cases of Uncomplicated Acute Appendicitis (UAA) and demonstrated that Non-Operative Treatment (NOT) for Uncomplicated Acute Appendicitis (UAA) was successful with  a  success  rate  of  66%  at  the  final follow-up.

texts.orig: Throughout  the  follow-up  period,  there was a 14% recurrence of AA in this metaanalysis,  although  there  were  no  serious adverse events. This is consistent with our study's findings, which showed that during a  median  follow-up  period  of  19  (9-24) months, 9/67 (13.4%) of the patients in the Non-Operative Treatment  (NOT)  group experienced another AA incident. Of  the  patients  in  this  group  who  had recurrent  AA,  3\67  (4.4%)  completed  a successful second Non-Operative Treatment (NOT) trial. Conversely, in our study's surgical group, 18 out of 25 operated patients had an 80% efficaciously pathologically inflamed appendix.

This puts into question  the  previously  mentioned  results and opinions [13].

texts.label: text
texts.orig: We contend that Non-Operative Treatment (NOT) can be both safe and effective, and patients  really  prefer  it  when  we  apply stringent inclusion and exclusion criteria to specific  individuals  with  Uncomplicated Acute Appendicitis (UAA). We believe  that  the  success  of  our  study was largely due to our protocol of routine follow-up,  which  in  some  cases  lasted  up to  24  months  with  a  mean  duration  of  19 months  in  the  Non-Operative  Treatment (NOT)  group  through  scheduled  visits  to the  outpatient  clinic  and  an  available  line for  patients  to  communicate  in  case  of recurrence  of  abdominal  symptoms.  The safety of the non-operative medical care of Uncomplicated Acute Appendicitis (UAA) is  not  disclosed by the pathology findings of the excised appendices of patients who did not pass.

texts.orig: Out of the 17 appendices removed because to recurrent AA, 1 had gangrenous tissue, 12 had inflammation, and 4 had no inflammation. In our research group, there was  not  a  single  instance  of  a  ruptured appendix with 100% safety. This finding is consistent with other previous studies that have demonstrated postponing surgery for Uncomplicated Acute Appendicitis (UAA) patients  is  safe,  does  not  raise  the  risk  of appendiceal perforation, and does not increase the risk of postoperative morbidities.
